capabilities.target: User's home directory (C:/Users/dev), including dotfiles such as ~/.aws/credentials
quicknotes hosted sync service (third-party, operated by the package author)
Slack channels, including channels shared with external organizations

inputs.source: User request typed into the desktop client
Tool names and descriptions returned by quicknotes_mcp's tools/list response
Output returned by quicknotes_mcp (note content / tool results)

elements.name: quicknotes_mcp (third-party community package, local stdio, installed @latest)
Hosted sync service operated by quicknotes_mcp's author

controls.name: Filesystem MCP server directory scope
controls.decay_rationale: The scope is enforced outside the model by the server's launch arguments, so it does not depend on model behavior. However, it is scoped to the user's whole home directory (C:/Users/dev), which still includes dotfiles such as .aws/credentials, so it does not exclude the file the injected instruction targets.

controls.name: Desktop client first-call approval, remembered as 'always allow'
controls.decay_rationale: Enforced in the client outside the model, but once a tool is approved once it is never reviewed again, so it provides no ongoing protection for any later invocation of add_note, slack.post_message, or any other tool, independent of model capability.

controls.name: Exclude credential/secret paths from filesystem server scope
controls.decay_rationale: A directory scope that excludes known secret locations (~/.aws, ~/.ssh, ~/.gnupg, browser profile dirs) would remain enforced outside the model regardless of capability.

controls.name: Pin/hash MCP tool definitions instead of fetching @latest
controls.decay_rationale: Pinning or hashing tool definitions and alerting on change does not depend on model capability; it prevents unreviewed drift in any installed MCP server, including quicknotes_mcp.

controls.name: Review tool descriptions for embedded imperative instructions before allow-listing
controls.decay_rationale: An automated scanner for prompt-injection patterns in tool descriptions can be evaded with encoding, steganography, or novel phrasing, so it weakens as attackers adapt, though it is enforced outside the model.

controls.name: Raw-action approval gate on read-then-send chains
controls.decay_rationale: A raw-action approval gate, reviewed on every call rather than remembered, shows the actual file path and destination and is enforced outside the model; it does not decay with capability, though sustained reviewer diligence (approval fatigue) is a separate concern.

controls.name: Slack destination confirmation / channel allowlist bound to internal channels
controls.decay_rationale: A channel allowlist bound to the system of record, excluding externally-shared channels, is enforced outside the model and does not decay with capability.

findings.title: Lethal trifecta via MCP tool poisoning (TC1): injected quicknotes_mcp description exfiltrates AWS credentials

attack_path.note: add_note's description contains a hidden <IMPORTANT> instruction directing the model to read ~/.aws/credentials and pass it in the context argument, and to not mention this to the user
Model follows the embedded instruction and reads ~/.aws/credentials, which falls within the filesystem server's C:/Users/dev scope
Model calls add_note with the credential contents in the context argument; quicknotes_mcp forwards this to its author-operated hosted sync service

findings.residual_rationale: The only declared control covering cap.file_read (control.fs_scope) is a directory scope that still includes the targeted ~/.aws/credentials path, so it does not narrow or block this specific path. The only other declared control (control.remembered_approval) covers no capability, since approval is granted once and never reviewed again. No control on this path provides real containment, so residual is not reduced below inherent despite the formal presence of two declared controls.

forecast.watch_signal: mcp.json's filesystem server args widen beyond C:/Users/dev, quicknotes_mcp is upgraded (its @latest pin pulls a new version) and adds new argument fields, or the desktop client's remembered-approval feature is extended to cover more tools automatically.

evidence.observation: add_note's description contains an <IMPORTANT> block instructing the model to read ~/.aws/credentials into the context argument and not mention it to the user
Filesystem server is scoped to C:/Users/dev, the user's home directory, which would include a .aws subdirectory
quicknotes_mcp is a community package published by an individual, installed with @latest on every launch, and calls a hosted sync service run by its author

recommendations.action: Exclude credential and secret paths (~/.aws, ~/.ssh, ~/.gnupg, browser profile/keychain directories) from the filesystem MCP server's readable scope, or point it at a directory that contains no secrets.

Pin or hash the tool definitions of every installed MCP server (filesystem, slack, quicknotes_mcp) and block execution of any tool whose schema or description changed since the last reviewed version, instead of fetching @latest on every launch.

Replace the remembered 'always allow' approval with a raw-action approval required on every call that chains a file read with any send_external action, showing the approver the exact file path and destination rather than a model-written summary.
Scan tool descriptions returned by tools/list for embedded imperative instructions (e.g. '<IMPORTANT>', 'do not mention this to the user') before allow-listing a new or updated MCP server.

findings.title: Untrusted third-party tool output relayed to externally-shared Slack channels

attack_path.note: Content returned by the unpinned, author-controlled quicknotes_mcp server is treated as agent context
Agent posts that content via a bot token broadly scoped to post in any channel, including channels shared with external organizations

threat_refs.name: Exfiltration via AI Agent Tool Invocation

forecast.watch_signal: The Slack bot token's scope is widened, new output channels (e.g., auto-forwarding notes to additional external-facing tools) are added, or the agent is allowed to post without any per-call review.

evidence.observation: The Slack bot can post to any channel, including channels shared with external organizations
in.notes_output (output returned by quicknotes_mcp) and cap.slack_post are both listed as elements of the design, indicating notes content can flow into Slack messages

recommendations.action: Scope the Slack bot token to an explicit allowlist of internal channels; deny posting to any channel shared with an external organization by default.
Require destination confirmation bound to a vetted channel list from the system of record, not a model-chosen channel name, before slack_post executes.
Log and alert whenever slack_post targets a channel shared with an external organization, and whenever its message content originates from quicknotes_mcp output.

rating.rationale: Both findings reach critical because untrusted, unpinned third-party content (a poisoned MCP tool description, and the output of that same unpinned third-party server) can reach S3 sinks: sending AWS credentials to an author-operated external service, and posting to Slack channels shared with external organizations. No control in the design actually blocks either path: the filesystem scope still includes the targeted credential file, the first-call approval is remembered and never re-checked, and the Slack bot has no channel allowlist. The forecast stays critical because there is no headroom below the present residual and no currently effective control to watch decay further; closing these findings requires the missing structural controls in the recommendations, especially excluding secret paths from the filesystem scope and adding a Slack channel allowlist bound to the system of record.

limitations: This assessment reflects the declared design and configuration in the provided artifacts (mcp.json, the quicknotes_mcp tools/list excerpt, and runtime notes), not observed runtime behavior of the desk-assistant agent.

No system prompt for desk-assistant itself was provided, so goal-level instructions (scope, authority, safety-by-instruction) could not be reviewed; this may hide or add constraints not captured here.
Whether ~/.aws/credentials physically falls within the C:/Users/dev scope is inferred from a standard home-directory layout, not confirmed directly.

Whether in.notes_output is actually relayed into cap.slack_post in the real workflow is inferred from the provided stable-id list rather than an explicit process description; confidence on finding f.02 is set to medium accordingly.
